name: Soldier's Requiem

detectability.signature: Faint tachyon residue consistent with temporal impression phenomena; visual manifestations on standard optics

proximity: Sensor ghosts appear on tactical displays, registering as vessel contacts that cannot be verified
Faint visual distortions become apparent, like heat shimmer, at approximately 300,000 km
Communication arrays pick up fragmentary transmissions on obsolete frequency bands
contact: Full visual manifestation of ancient battle replays visible through viewports and optical sensors
Phantom weapons fire registers on shield and threat detection systems, triggering false alarms
Crew experience mild temporal disorientation, losing track of minutes at a time
prolonged_exposure: Temporal echoes begin to interact with ship systems, causing phantom damage readings
Crew members report difficulty distinguishing echo events from real-time events
Mild but persistent temporal displacement headaches affecting sensitive individuals

age: The echoed event dates to approximately 8,700 years ago; the echo phenomenon itself is self-sustaining

behavior.cycle: Full battle replay cycles every 73 hours, with fragmentary echoes occurring continuously between cycles

phenomena: Ghostly fleets of warships from an unknown civilization engage in a battle that replays with perfect consistency
The echoed vessels number approximately 400, spanning at least two distinct technological traditions
One fleet is systematically destroyed in each replay; the victors then turn on each other in apparent mutiny
The final echo in each cycle is a single vessel drifting, dark and silent, before the replay resets
hazards: False threat readings from phantom weapons fire can trigger automated defensive systems
Temporal disorientation may impair crew judgment during extended observation
The echo zone overlaps with a minor shipping lane, occasionally startling unprepared crews
opportunities: The echo preserves a complete record of a battle fought by an unknown civilization 8,700 years ago
Study of the echoed weapons and ship designs offers insight into extinct military technologies
The self-sustaining nature of the echo could advance understanding of temporal impression mechanics
known_incidents: A passenger liner transiting the zone in 3141 triggered a ship-wide panic when the echo's battle replay manifested around the vessel during a full cycle; the incident led to the zone's addition to standard navigation charts and its current name, chosen by the liner's captain as a mark of respect for the ancient dead
description: Soldier's Requiem is a ghost story written in light and time. Across a volume of space 840,000 kilometers wide, the final battle of an unknown civilization replays itself every 73 hours with mechanical precision. Ghostly warships shimmer into existence, their hulls bearing designs that match no known culture, their weapons firing silent volleys of phantom energy. The visual fidelity is remarkable, down to the venting of atmosphere from breached hulls and the tumbling of debris that fades before it drifts beyond the zone's boundary.

The echo replays the same sequence without variation. Two fleets of roughly 200 ships each engage in a pitched battle lasting approximately four hours. One fleet is methodically destroyed. Then, in the replay's most haunting passage, the victorious fleet turns upon itself, ships firing on their former allies in what appears to be a sudden and total mutiny. The cycle ends with a single vessel drifting dark and powerless, the last survivor of a war that consumed both sides. Then silence, until the next cycle begins.

The battle occurred approximately 8,700 years ago, and neither the civilizations involved nor the cause of the conflict has been identified. The echo is self-sustaining, fed by a temporal impression so violent that it scarred the fabric of spacetime itself. Its name was given by the captain of a passenger liner whose unexpected transit through a full battle cycle caused widespread panic among passengers. She named it Soldier's Requiem, arguing that whatever those ancient crews had fought and died for deserved at least the dignity of remembrance.

Soldier's Requiem is now a charted navigational feature and, unexpectedly, a minor pilgrimage destination. Veterans, historians, and the simply curious visit the zone to witness the replay, and a small observation platform maintains position at the boundary. The echo shows no signs of fading, its temporal impression as sharp today as it must have been millennia ago. Researchers continue to study the echoed vessels and weapons, slowly assembling a picture of the two civilizations that destroyed each other here. The identity of the lone surviving ship, and whether it carried anyone away from this place, remains unknown.
